clue.text: Before 5050, space explorers ultimately pay through the nose (7)

blocks.note: the American space agency — the crossword's standard explorers
fifty is L in Roman numerals, so fifty-fifty is LL
the final letter of paY

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a complaint about prices and the answer is about anatomy. Two conventions to bank here: L is fifty in Roman numerals, and 'ultimately' asks for a word's last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sounds made nasally come out through the nose rather than the mouth, so the adverb and the phrase name the same route.

clue.text: Foolish like 1 + 9? (7)

blocks.note: 'like' = as, the plainest comparison in the language
the Roman numeral for one
the digit taken as its own name

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like arithmetic and it is spelling: a numeral can stand for its Roman letter or for the word we say out loud, and this clue uses one of each.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine comes from asinus, the Latin donkey, so calling an idea asinine says it is stupid in the particular braying way an ass is.

clue.text: I earn change importing without charge or latitude (1,4,4)

blocks.note: five letters rearranged into A REIN, which then opens up
free = at no charge, and it is imported into the middle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' shuffles the two words in front of it and 'importing' brings something in, so the surface's customs declaration is doing two mechanical jobs at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Give someone a free rein and you give them latitude: the picture is a rider slackening the reins so the horse chooses its own line.

clue.text: Extra line to say farewell (3,3)

blocks.note: a leg is one straight stretch of a route or a journey
bye is the shortest goodbye there is

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket hides in plain sight: the definition is the single word 'Extra', and the two everyday words after it are simply laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket an extra is a run scored without the bat touching the ball, and a leg bye — deflected off the batter's body — is one kind.

clue.text: Substitute case of stout with case of brandy (5-2)

blocks.note: the case of a word is its outside: STouT
with = and, the joiner taken at face value as letters
BrandY, outside only

explanation.walkthrough: Both drinks come in cases in the packing sense — keep the outside, drop the contents — and the little word between them is not joinery at all but three letters of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand-by is the spare kept ready to take someone's place, so 'Substitute' names it by the job it is waiting to do.

clue.text: Heart admits nothing against being idle (4,4)

blocks.note: the heart is the body's ticker, and it opens to let two letters in
the round letter is the crossword's zero
v for versus, as on any fixture list

explanation.walkthrough: 'Admits' is the container signal — something is let inside — and the surface's medical hush is hiding an engine turning over in a car park.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine ticking over is running but going nowhere, which is what 'idle' means of machinery: the verb, not the adjective about laziness.

clue.text: Point revealed by 14 or 13? (5)

blocks.note: spell the number out — fourteeN — and keep its last letter
the clue's own 'or', taken as two letters
THirteen, spelled out, leads with these two

explanation.walkthrough: Write the numerals out as words and the answer is lying across the join: fourtee | n or th | irteen. Nothing else in the clue does any work, which is what makes it hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A compass has four cardinal points, and this is the one every map is drawn around, so 'Point' names it by class.

clue.text: Worries relatives when first king abdicates (7)

blocks.note: brothers are relatives
R is Rex, the king — and the clue says it is the first of the word's two Rs

explanation.walkthrough: Abdication is a neat deletion signal: the king steps down and leaves the word. Note that the clue has to say which R, because there are two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: To bother someone is to nag at them mildly, and 'Worries' catches the same low-level, persistent fretting rather than any real alarm.

clue.text: Dan perhaps mixing art material – it’s missing base (7,6)

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder
three more, the apostrophe ignored
e is the base of natural logarithms, and it is the letter taken out

explanation.walkthrough: Fourteen letters go in and thirteen come out, so something has to leave before the shuffle, and 'base' is the mathematician's e. The art student is pure misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: In judo and karate a dan is the black-belt grade, so naming the rank points at the person holding it — which is what 'perhaps' concedes.

clue.text: Locale for Derrick’s young lady? ‘I love travelling west’ (3,3)

blocks.note: Derrick's girl, in the surface story at least
the clue's own I
love is nothing on a tennis scoreboard — a zero

explanation.walkthrough: Two derricks in one clue: the man in the surface and the drilling tower in the answer. 'Travelling west' reverses an across entry, reading it right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: A derrick is the tower standing over a well, so the rig is the place you find one — the definition names a location by its equipment.

clue.text: A Catholic member of the clergy is faithful (8)

blocks.note: the clue's own A
C is the standard abbreviation, as in RC
a curate is a junior parish priest

explanation.walkthrough: Three pieces laid end to end with no indicator at all, which is the hardest charade to spot: nothing in the sentence admits that anything is being built.
explanation.definitionFit: A faithful copy or translation reports its original exactly, and that is the sense of accurate wanted here — true to something, not merely right.

clue.text: Prevent Shakespeare forgetting Bottom (3)

blocks.note: Shakespeare's popular nickname, ending in a D, supplies the source word for the wordplay
the wordplay drops the last letter of that nickname

explanation.walkthrough: Bottom is a Shakespeare character and a position in a word at the same time, and the clue means the second while pointing at the first.
explanation.definitionFit: To bar someone from a place is to prevent them entering — the verb behind 'barred from', nothing to do with the drinking sort.

clue.text: Woe is me! Reckless and extremely risky (6)

blocks.note: four letters, recklessly rearranged
the extremes of the word — its first and last letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Woe is me' is one exclamation in the surface and two separate jobs in the parse: the definition stops dead after the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Misery is woe felt over time — a settled state rather than a single cry of grief — but the two nouns are plain synonyms.

clue.text: Degenerates wanting Academy Awards (8)

blocks.note: to atrophy is to waste away, to degenerate
A = Academy, as in the RA

explanation.walkthrough: The Oscars are all over the surface and nowhere in the parse: 'Academy' is worth exactly one letter, and 'Awards' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A trophy is the cup or statuette handed over at a prizegiving, so 'Awards' names them by the ceremony rather than the object.

clue.text: Measure English trout initially found in French sea (5)

blocks.note: la mer — the wrapper
E is the usual abbreviation for English
the first letter of trout

explanation.walkthrough: MER for the French sea is worth banking: it turns up constantly, and almost always wrapped around something. The angler is here only to supply one initial.
explanation.definitionFit: To meter something is to measure it out, which is what a gas or parking meter does all day, so the device and the verb both answer to 'Measure'.

clue.text: Man seeks new drug to hold water (4,5)

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder, straight out of the lonely-hearts column
E for ecstasy, the crossword's default drug

explanation.walkthrough: 'New' sits between the fodder and the extra letter, shuffling both together. The surface reads as a small ad taking a dark turn, and the answer is an idiom about arguments.
explanation.definitionFit: An argument that holds water has no leaks in it, so the definition is a whole-phrase idiom rather than a synonym for either word.

clue.text: Add more detail to complex (9)

blocks.note: the verb: when asked, you supply more detail beyond what you've already given
the adjective: describes something with many finely worked, interlocking parts

explanation.walkthrough: One spelling, two pronunciations: the verb ends like 'rate', the adjective swallows the ending. The split falls after 'detail', with 'to' as the only joinery.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to add detail to what you have said; as an adjective it describes something intricate and heavily worked — complex.

clue.text: Celts ski, going downhill with the most smooth manner (8)

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder
surface only: it gives the skiers something to be smooth in, and no letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Going downhill' does two jobs at once — it is what skiers do, and deterioration is the standard image behind an anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Slick means smooth to the point of frictionless, so the superlative is the smoothest of the lot, with a hint that it is too smooth to trust.

clue.text: Personal number key during father’s rejected US medical procedure (6,3)

blocks.note: PA'S — father's — thrown back to make the wrapper
a PIN is literally a personal identification number
the Alt key, on every keyboard

explanation.walkthrough: Two pieces go inside at once, and the wrapper is a possessive turned round: PA'S becomes SAP. Nothing here is about the band, or about the spine.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinal tap is the American name for drawing fluid from the spine, which in Britain is a lumbar puncture — hence the flagged nationality.

clue.text: 7 star submarine (7)

blocks.note: solve 7 down first: the star that marks that compass point
these Royal Navy submarines took their name from the missile system they carried, itself named for the Pole Star

explanation.walkthrough: A cross-reference: 7 down has to fall first. Both halves then point at one word from opposite worlds, celestial navigation and the cold war.
explanation.definitionFit: Polaris is the pole star sitting almost exactly above the earth's axis, and it named the missile — and so the boats — of Britain's cold-war deterrent.

clue.text: Prince arrived in Hungary on vacation (5)

blocks.note: vacated — emptied out — so only the outer letters stay
arr. is the timetable's abbreviation for arrived

explanation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' means vacated rather than sunbathing, a pun worth keeping: a country on holiday loses everything inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The best-known bearer of the name is a prince of the British royal family, so the clue defines by example rather than by meaning.

clue.text: They steal over 2 billion euros, not even starting with rupees (7)

blocks.note: the letter it starts with
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
billion is B, and the clue asks for two of them
'not even' keeps the odd letters only: EuRoS

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not even' is the alternate-letter instruction and 'starting with' says where the R goes rather than what it is. Three currencies, none of them worth any money here.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is a small sentence rather than a noun: people who steal are robbers, and the plural pronoun keeps it in step with the answer.

clue.text: Second-tier attractions, those with trains? (6)

blocks.note: the second tier of any grading is the B list
the attractions at a funfair are its rides

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter admitting that not every one of them wears a train, and the railway sense of the word is the trap.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedding gown's train is the length of fabric trailing behind the wearer, so the definition points at the women wearing them.

clue.text: Stray lately wandering around California (5,3)

blocks.note: six letters rearranged, and they then close around the state
the two-letter postal abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters split around CA, which is why the answer's two words do not line up with the clue's — the seam falls inside the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An alley cat is the archetypal stray: no owner, no home, living off bins in the back streets, so the definition names it by what it lacks.

clue.text: Wise one in Munich on retreat drinking last of beer? (5)

blocks.note: 'one' in the German of Munich, before it turns round
the final letter of beeR

explanation.walkthrough: Munich sets the language rather than the map: the clue wants the German for one. The beer belongs to the surface and supplies a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernie Wise was half of Morecambe and Wise, so the surname stands in for the first name — a definition by example.

clue.text: Greek character married bachelor, one with diamonds? (6)

blocks.note: the seventeenth letter of the Greek alphabet
M, as on any form
B is the crossword's bachelor, from the degree
the Roman numeral

explanation.walkthrough: Three of the four pieces come out of the abbreviation drawer: married, bachelor and one are all doing letter duty rather than describing anybody.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhombus is the diamond shape of a playing-card suit or a kite, and rhombi is its Latin plural — the shapes, not the gems.

clue.text: British company once part of public infrastructure (3)

blocks.note: the letters straddle the gap: publIC Infrastructure

explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of' is the signal that something is buried in the words that follow, and three letters across a word break is where the eye refuses to look.
explanation.definitionFit: ICI was Imperial Chemical Industries, a giant of British manufacturing until it was broken up and sold — which is what 'once' is doing.

clue.text: Royal papers describing metal crown missing (8)

blocks.note: the press is the papers, collectively — the wrapper
one of the commoner metals
the crown of ZINC is its top letter, and it goes, so only INC is described

explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' means drawing around, as you describe a circle — a container signal, not a definition one. The crown of a word is the letter on top of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A princess is a royal by birth or by marriage, and 'Royal' is the adjective used as the noun it has become in the papers.

clue.text: Trader: ‘Expensive coats, Levi’s – 60% off!’ (6)

blocks.note: dear = expensive, and it coats what comes next
the jeans, five letters
three of those five letters — sixty per cent — are knocked off the price

explanation.walkthrough: A sale sign doing arithmetic: sixty per cent off five letters leaves two, and they are the two at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer trades in something for a living — cars, art, anything — so 'Trader' is a plain synonym with a slightly shadier ring to it.

clue.text: American to highlight revolting states (7)

blocks.note: A = American, the dictionary's own label
STRESS, to highlight, turned round

explanation.walkthrough: The surface promises rebellious states and delivers none: 'revolting' is a reversal, and the states are the definition rather than the scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: To assert something is to state it flatly, as fact and without argument, so the verb form matches the definition exactly.

clue.text: ‘Snake’ – language of slander (7)

blocks.note: the asp is the crossword's snake of choice
Erse is Irish Gaelic, a regular in these grids

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks warn that 'Snake' is not being used for its meaning. Erse is worth banking: four letters, a language, and endlessly useful to setters.
explanation.definitionFit: To asperse someone is to cast aspersions on them — a formal verb that survives mainly inside that noun phrase.
